title: Best DORA Metrics Tools for Engineering Leaders in 2026
summary: Compare DORA metrics tools by data sources, metric definitions, and setup. See how delivery dashboards and Weave’s code output analysis fit together.
body_markdown:
## TL;DR


- Choose a DORA metrics tool by the production deployments and incidents it can explain in your environment. A dashboard built from incomplete events can give a precise answer to the wrong question.
- GitLab suits teams whose delivery and incident data already live there. Datadog connects delivery measurement with observability. Apache DevLake offers a self-hosted dashboard. DX combines system data with developer feedback.
- Weave adds code-based output, review, quality, and AI measurement alongside deployment metrics. Check each metric’s definition: a successful deployment job, a reliable production release, and a substantial engineering change describe different results.


Weave publishes this guide. The comparison uses the first-party documentation linked below, checked October 16, 2026. It is a shortlist by use case, not a performance ranking. No vendor’s dashboard was independently benchmarked for this article.


## What should a DORA metrics dashboard measure?


A release can contain a configuration fix or a major migration. Deployment frequency counts a release either way. That makes it useful for understanding delivery flow, while leaving the scope and outcome of the work for other measures.


Start with the current framework.[DORA’s official guide](https://dora.dev/guides/dora-metrics/) defines **five software delivery performance metrics** :


Scroll horizontally if needed →


Metric What to establish before comparing tools


Change lead time The time from a committed code change to its production deployment


Deployment frequency The production deployments counted within the reporting window


Failed deployment recovery time The time to recover from a deployment that needs immediate intervention


Change fail rate The share of deployments that require immediate intervention


Deployment rework rate The share of deployments that are unplanned responses to production incidents


Many products still document the earlier four-metric model. Some also retain the label “MTTR” or “time to restore service.” Ask which failures start the clock and which event stops it. A deployment failure, an incident, and an outage from another cause can produce different recovery measures.


Use DORA at the application or service level and follow the same service over time. Its[guidance on common pitfalls](https://dora.dev/guides/dora-metrics/#common-pitfalls) cautions against comparing unrelated applications or turning metric targets into competition.


## DORA metrics tools compared


Scroll horizontally if needed →


Tool Consider it when Documented measurement approach Validate in your trial


**GitLab** Your team already uses GitLab for production delivery Deployment and merge request data, with GitLab incidents for failure and recovery measures Production environment classification, incident coverage, and merge-to-deploy lead time


**Datadog** Delivery analysis needs to sit beside service observability Deployment events from APM or API/CLI, Git metadata, and configured failure detection Service tags, repository synchronization, and failure detection rules


**Apache DevLake** Your platform team wants to own the data pipeline and dashboard Connected source control, deployment and incident records, with Grafana dashboards Scope rules, ingestion maintenance, and the SQL behind each panel


**DX** You want system-based delivery data and developer feedback Self-reported snapshots or system-based reports connected through service ownership Deployment attribution, incident identifiers, and the lead-time report selected


**Weave** You want to connect delivery health with code output and AI investment Production deployment metrics alongside code analysis, reviews, quality, and AI measurement Production workflow settings, merge-to-deploy timing, and deployment recovery semantics


The setup details matter more than a checkmark for “DORA supported.” For every candidate, ask whether deployment rework rate is available in the proposed configuration. The four-metric documentation linked here does not establish complete coverage of DORA’s current five-metric framework.


### GitLab: start with the delivery data you already have


[GitLab’s DORA documentation](https://docs.gitlab.com/user/analytics/dora_metrics/) explains its calculations in detail. Deployment frequency counts successful production deployments. Its lead time for changes starts when a merge request merges, rather than when the code was first committed.


The failure and recovery calculations depend on GitLab incident records. If incidents live elsewhere, confirm how they reach those records before treating an empty failure chart as evidence of reliable releases.


**Trial question:** Can you trace a release and its incident through the same reporting window, and explain why the deployment appears in the chart?


### Datadog: connect delivery changes with service health


[Datadog DORA Metrics](https://docs.datadoghq.com/dora_metrics/) supports filtering delivery results by service, team, repository, environment, and time period. That fits teams investigating delivery alongside production health.


Its[setup guide](https://docs.datadoghq.com/dora_metrics/setup/) describes deployment ingestion through APM Deployment Tracking or its API/CLI. Change lead time also needs Git metadata and repository synchronization. Failure detection has its own configuration, so installing an observability agent alone does not establish complete DORA measurement.


**Trial question:** Does the production deployment include the right commit and service identity, and does the failure detector classify a known bad release correctly?


### Apache DevLake: own the collection and calculations


[Apache DevLake](https://devlake.apache.org/docs/DORA/) connects engineering data and provides a DORA dashboard in Grafana. Teams define deployment and incident scope, associate their connections with a project, and can inspect or customize the SQL behind the panels.


It can ingest deployment and incident events through webhooks when a connector does not cover the source. This flexibility comes with operational work: someone must maintain the installation, ingestion, scope definitions, and dashboard queries.


**Trial question:** Who will investigate a missing deployment or a broken connector after the initial setup, and can they reproduce the displayed metric from its underlying records?


### DX: combine delivery instrumentation with developer feedback


[DX documents two DORA setup paths](https://docs.getdx.com/reports/dora-metrics/) : self-reported snapshots and system-based measurement. The latter needs source control, deployment, incident, and service ownership data. Its reports distinguish PR-open-to-deploy, merge-to-deploy, and commit-to-deploy timing.


DX also documents[complexity-weighted throughput in its Catalog analysis](https://docs.getdx.com/reports/catalog-analysis/) when AI tools are enabled. Buyers should compare the actual output model and available evidence, rather than assume every competing platform only counts PRs.


**Trial question:** Are deployment and incident records mapped to the same service, and is the report using survey responses or connected system events?


### Weave: inspect the work behind the delivery trend


[Weave Engineering Intelligence](https://weaveos.com/products/engineering-intelligence) combines deployment metrics with code output, reviews, reverts, churn, and AI contribution signals.[Silk 1](https://weaveos.com/products/code-intelligence) reads code changes and estimates the work in a common unit of expert engineering effort. Its scores include reasoning and support team calibration.


This lets a leader investigate whether faster delivery accompanies a change in the work shipped. A higher release count could reflect smaller batches, more fixes, or a different project mix. Code output and quality give that discussion more context. They do not establish customer value or prove that AI caused an improvement.


Weave’s published delivery measures include deployment frequency, deployment success rate, deploy MTTR, and PR deploy lead time. Their definitions are worth checking closely:


- **PR deploy lead time starts at merge.** It is not the same interval as DORA’s commit-to-production lead time.
- **Deployment success rate describes deployment completion.** Its inverse is not automatically the share of releases that cause a production incident.
- **Deploy MTTR measures failed-deployment-to-next-successful-deployment time.** It should not be treated as incident resolution time without checking those events against the incident record.


Use those measures for the questions they answer. For procurement that requires every current DORA metric, validate the exact configuration and event evidence in the trial.


**Trial question:** Can you inspect the code, output explanation, review history, and production deployment behind the same change?


## Keep delivery, output, and business outcomes separate


A useful engineering review can answer several questions without collapsing them into one score:


Scroll horizontally if needed →


Question Evidence to inspect


Are changes reaching production safely? Deployments, incidents, recovery, and rework


What engineering work shipped? Code changes, scope, output estimates, and review context


Is quality holding up? Reverts, defects, churn, review findings, and production behavior


Is AI investment helping? Adoption and cost alongside output, quality, and delivery over comparable periods


Did customers benefit? Product usage, reliability, customer feedback, and the relevant business outcome


Weave’s[Q2 2026 research report](https://weaveos.com/research/q2-2026) illustrates why activity and output should be examined separately: it analyzes PR volume alongside code-based output rather than treating them as interchangeable. Those observational findings are context for a measurement plan, not a guarantee of a result for your team.


For AI budget decisions, the[AI ROI measurement guide](https://weaveos.com/blog/ai-roi-measurement-tools-for-engineering-teams) explains how spending, adoption, output, and quality fit together. Keep the service, team, time window, and cost basis consistent when comparing a change.


## How to run a useful buying trial


Choose one production service and a reporting period that includes a normal release and a release requiring remediation. If no failed release exists in the sample, mark recovery and failure measures as untested. Do not interpret missing incidents as a zero failure rate.


1. **Agree on event definitions.** Record what counts as production, the lead-time start, the failure condition, the recovery event, and an unplanned remediation deployment.
2. **Reconcile the records.** Compare the tool with the release log and incident system. Account for staging runs, duplicate events, rollbacks, and changes spanning several services.
3. **Inspect a metric’s inputs.** Open a deployment, identify its commits or PRs, and follow a linked incident. Check missing-data behavior and aggregation rules.
4. **Investigate one constraint.** Decide whether the next action is reducing review delay, removing release friction, improving tests, or changing incident response. A dashboard should support that decision.
5. **Check ownership and cost.** Confirm the required plan, connectors, permissions, data retention, exports, and ongoing maintenance with each vendor. Compare the full operating cost rather than an unverified list price.


When evaluating Weave, include a feature, a fix, and a refactor in the code sample. Read the output explanations and ask engineers whether the scores reflect the work. Then inspect delivery and quality around those changes.

## Frequently asked questions


### What is the best DORA metrics tool?


The right choice depends on your delivery data and the decision you need to make. Start with GitLab if its deployment and incident records already cover your workflow. Consider Datadog for observability, DevLake for a self-hosted pipeline, DX for combined system and developer feedback, and Weave for delivery context alongside code output and AI measurement. Validate the same service in each trial.


### Can Git data alone produce a complete DORA dashboard?


Git history identifies code changes. Complete delivery measurement also needs reliable production deployment and failure evidence. A merge is not proof that code reached users. Confirm how each tool obtains the missing events and labels any inferred data.


### Are DORA metrics and engineering output the same thing?


They answer different questions. DORA describes delivery performance. Code output analysis examines the work inside changes. Customer and business outcomes need their own evidence. Use them together when evaluating an engineering investment.


### Does a four-metric dashboard cover the current framework?


Not necessarily. DORA’s current guide includes deployment rework rate as a fifth metric. Ask for the definition, event source, and a worked example for each required measure, including recovery metrics with older names.
